# Sinusitis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Infectious diseases > Infections of the pharynx and respiratory tract > Sinusitis*

[Original Article Link](/library/sj0tbT)

---

## Summary

Rhinosinusitis is a <u>mucosal</u> inflammation of both the <u>paranasal sinuses</u> and adjacent nasal cavities. Viral infection is the most common cause of <u>acute rhinosinusitis</u> (<u>ARS</u>); bacterial and <u>fungal infections</u> also occur. The characteristic <u>symptoms of rhinosinusitis</u> are <u>purulent</u> <u>rhinorrhea</u>, nasal obstruction, and facial <u>pain</u>. <u>ARS</u> is often <u>self-limiting</u>, but <u>antibiotic therapy</u> may be indicated in the case of suspected or diagnosed bacterial <u>superinfection</u>. Imaging and endoscopy are reserved for patients with <u>recurrent sinusitis</u>, <u>red flags for rhinosinusitis</u>, or certain <u>risk factors</u> (e.g., <u>immunosuppression</u>). Rarely, the infection may spread to the <u>soft tissues</u>, bone, vascular system, and/or <u>central nervous system</u>. <u>Chronic rhinosinusitis</u> (<u>CRS</u>), a chronic inflammatory state similar to <u>asthma</u>, lasts at least 12 weeks and may be complicated by bacterial exacerbations or chronic <u>fungal infections</u>. Diagnosis is confirmed by findings of inflammation on imaging, <u>anterior rhinoscopy</u>, or <u>nasal endoscopy</u>. Underlying comorbidities, such as <u>allergy</u>, <u>cystic fibrosis</u>, and <u>immunodeficiency</u>, should be ruled out. First-line treatment of <u>CRS</u> is intranasal <u>steroids</u> and nasal <u>irrigation</u> for symptomatic relief. Patients with persistent symptoms may require <u>surgery</u>.

---

## Definitions

* Pansinusitis: inflammation of all sinuses on one or both sides

* Acute sinusitis: inflammation of the sinuses for < 4 weeks

* Subacute sinusitis: progressive symptoms of sinus inflammation occurring over 4–12 weeks; represents a transition from acute to chronic infection

* Chronic sinusitis: persistent symptoms of sinus inflammation > 12 weeks

* Recurrent acute sinusitis: four or more separate episodes of <u>acute sinusitis</u> that occur within 1 year, with at least 8 weeks of symptom resolution between episodes

* Rhinosinusitis: simultaneous inflammation of the nasal <u>mucosa</u> and sinuses





References:[[1]](/library/ys0dxh)[[2]](/library/dG0oyh)

---

## Epidemiology

* <u>Incidence</u>: Sinusitis is one of the most commonly diagnosed conditions in the US, affecting an estimated 35 million individuals per year.

* Peak <u>incidence</u>: early fall to early spring

* Sex: <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u>





References:[[3]](/library/ZG0ZBh)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

* Pathogens

* Viral (most common): <u>rhinovirus</u>, <u>coronavirus</u>, <u>adenovirus</u>, <u>influenza</u>, and <u>parainfluenza viruses</u>

* Bacterial: particularly <u>S. pneumoniae</u>, <u>H. influenzae</u>, <u>M. catarrhalis</u>, <u>S. aureus</u>, <u>E. coli</u>, and <u>Klebsiella</u>.

* Fungal: e.g., <u>Aspergillus</u>, <u>Rhizopus oryzae</u>

* Route of transmission: <u>droplet transmission</u>, particularly in winter months

* <u>Risk factors</u>

* Preexisting viral <u>upper respiratory tract infection</u> (<u>URTI</u>): most common; leads to superimposed bacterial infections

* Ventilation disorders of the sinuses

* <u>Hypertrophy</u> of <u>nasal turbinates</u>, <u>nasal polyps</u>, <u>deviation of nasal septum</u>

* Impairments of ciliary function such as <u>cystic fibrosis</u>, <u>primary ciliary dyskinesia</u>, <u>granulomatosis with polyangiitis</u>, allergic inflammation , and <u>immunodeficiency</u>

* <u>Concha bullosa</u> (also known as a <u>middle turbinate pneumatization</u>)

* Foreign body lodged in the nasal cavity (particularly seen in children).

* <u>Odontogenic infection</u>: leads to unilateral maxillary sinusitis

* <u>Rhinitis</u>: spread of pathogens via nasal <u>mucosa</u>

* <u>Bronchial asthma</u>

* <u>Analgesic</u> (<u>NSAIDs</u>, <u>aspirin</u>) intolerance





![Concha bullosa](media/tqkrqxiz3v7qjsiblg8pg632.jpg)

Concha bullosa




References:[[4]](/library/mxbVCD)

## Pathophysiology

* Sinusitis is triggered by three factors: obstruction of sinus drainage pathways (sinus ostia) due to <u>mucosal</u> <u>edema</u>, ciliary impairment, and altered mucus quantity and quality → stasis of secretions inside the sinuses → <u>proliferation</u> of various pathogens;   → sinusitis

* Recurrent, untreated/complicated <u>acute sinusitis</u> may lead to <u>chronic sinusitis</u>.





References:[[5]](/library/5xbiCD)

---

## Clinical features

### <u>Acute rhinosinusitis</u> [[6]](/library/UG0bAh)




#### <u>Rhinitis</u>




* Sneezing, nasal congestion, <u>rhinorrhea</u>, and <u>postnasal drip</u>

* <u>Hyposmia</u>/<u>anosmia</u>





#### Sinusitis




* Unspecific symptoms: <u>fever</u> (∼ 50% of cases), <u>headaches</u>, general <u>malaise</u>, <u>myalgia</u>

* Facial <u>pain</u>/pressure, <u>erythema</u>, and swelling over the affected area due to inflammation 

* <u>Maxillary sinuses</u> are most commonly affected.

* Since maxillary ostium, which drains the <u>maxillary sinuses</u>, is located posteriorly and medially near the roof of the <u>maxillary sinus</u>, secretions are drained against the pull of gravity (i.e., upward), causing secretions to accumulate and increasing the susceptibility to infection.

* Inflammation of <u>mucosa</u> → sinus ostial blockage → drainage into the ostiomeatal complex → ↑ mucus production by the nasal <u>mucosa</u> → congestion and swelling of the nasal passages → sinus cavity <u>hypoxia</u> and mucus retention → ↓ function of nasal <u>cilia</u> → ↓ transportation of mucus and debris from the nose → creation of ideal conditions for bacterial growth → ↑ susceptibility to infection

* Manifests with <u>pain</u> in <u>jaw</u> region (mimics <u>dental pain</u>)

* <u>Frontal sinuses</u>: <u>pain</u> in the lower forehead

* <u>Ethmoidal sinuses</u>: <u>pain</u> in the nasal bridge region or retroorbital <u>pain</u>

* <u>Sphenoid sinuses</u>: located in the <u>sphenoid</u> bones near the <u>optic nerve</u> and <u>pituitary gland</u>

* <u>Transillumination</u> may show opacification.





#### Subtypes




* Acute viral rhinosinusitis

* May occur with <u>acute otitis media</u>

* May manifest with other <u>symptoms of URTI</u> (e.g., <u>sore throat</u>, <u>cough</u>)

* Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis

* Severe symptoms (including <u>fever</u> > 39Â°C, facial <u>pain</u>, <u>purulent</u> nasal discharge)

* Symptoms typically remain stable or improve for 5–6 days and then worsen (double worsening).

* <u>Fungal rhinosinusitis</u> is discussed in “Subtypes and variants.” [[4]](/library/mxbVCD)





### <u>Chronic rhinosinusitis</u> [[6]](/library/UG0bAh)




<u>Chronic rhinosinusitis</u> can manifest acutely with exacerbation of symptoms or take an insidious course with low-grade symptoms persisting over months to years.




* Symptoms

* Facial <u>pain</u>

* Mucopurulent drainage (<u>anterior</u>, <u>posterior</u>, or both)

* <u>Anosmia</u> or <u>hyposmia</u>

* Nasal congestion

* Signs of inflammation

* <u>Purulent</u> mucus or <u>edema</u> in the <u>middle meatus</u>/<u>anterior</u> ethmoidal area seen in <u>anterior rhinoscopy</u>

* Polyps in the nasal cavity/<u>middle meatus</u>





#### Subtypes




* <u>Chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis</u> is discussed in “Subtypes and variants.”

* Chronic <u>fungal rhinosinusitis</u> is discussed in “Subtypes and variants.”

* <u>Chronic rhinosinusitis</u> without <u>nasal polyps</u>: Pathogenesis is associated with anatomical abnormalities (e.g., septal deviation, tumors) and dental disease (i.e., sinusitis of dental origin).

---

## Subtypes and variants

### Chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis[[6]](/library/UG0bAh)[[7]](/library/dvdo_70)[[8]](/library/ytddT70)




Nasal polyps are benign lesions of the nasal <u>mucosa</u> or <u>paranasal sinuses</u> that develop due to chronic <u>mucosal</u> inflammation, commonly in the context of <u>chronic rhinosinusitis</u>.




#### Clinical features




* Typical features

* <u>Anterior</u> <u>rhinorrhea</u> or <u>postnasal drip</u>

* Bilateral nasal obstruction

* Impaired olfactory function (from hyposmia to anosmia)

* Facial <u>pain</u> and/or pressure

* <u>Sleep</u> disturbance

* Associated conditions

* <u>Cystic fibrosis</u>

* <u>Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease</u> (<u>AERD</u>): triad of <u>asthma</u>, <u>chronic sinusitis</u> with recurrent <u>nasal polyps</u>, and <u>sensitivity</u> to <u>aspirin</u> and other <u>NSAIDs</u>





#### Diagnostics




See “<u>Diagnostics for rhinosinusitis</u>” for details.




* Diagnosis requires <u>diagnostic criteria for chronic rhinosinusitis</u> plus visualized polyps.

* Findings on <u>diagnostics for chronic rhinosinusitis</u> include:

* <u>Nasal endoscopy</u>: yellow, white, or pink masses with a grape-like appearance

* CT: exact location and extent of polyps

* <u>Biopsy</u>: tissue <u>eosinophilia</u>

* Consider additional testing to evaluate for associated conditions, e.g.:

* <u>Diagnostics for cystic fibrosis</u>

* Diagnostics for <u>asthma</u>





> [!TIP]
> Perform <u>diagnostics for cystic fibrosis</u> in patients who have <u>nasal polyps</u> if they are < 18 years of age or have refractory rhinosinusitis. [[9]](/library/fD0kdR)




#### Differential diagnosis [[10]](/library/VvdG_70)




* Benign nasal lesions, e.g.:

* Choanal polyp: a large unilateral <u>nasal polyp</u> that originates in the <u>mucous membrane</u> of the <u>maxillary sinus</u> and grows into the nasal cavity and <u>nasopharynx</u> [[11]](/library/7Ed4C70)

* <u>Nasal papilloma</u>

* <u>Mucocele</u>

* <u>Encephalocele</u>

* Cavernous <u>hemangioma</u>

* <u>Malignancy</u>, e.g.:

* <u>Squamous cell carcinoma</u>

* <u>Lymphoma</u>





#### Treatment [[10]](/library/VvdG_70)[[12]](/library/WvdP_70)




See “<u>Treatment of rhinosinusitis</u>” for details, including dosages.




* All patients: topical <u>corticosteroids</u> (e.g., spray or rinse) and nasal saline <u>irrigation</u>

* Consider short course (< 3 weeks) of oral <u>corticosteroids</u> for patients with: [[6]](/library/UG0bAh)[[13]](/library/Y6Xnj_)

* Inadequate response to topical therapy after 3 months

* Severe symptoms

* Alternative treatment options (e.g., if initial therapy is ineffective or contraindicated) include:  

* <u>Macrolides</u> (e.g., <u>azithromycin</u>)

* <u>Leukotriene-receptor antagonists</u> (e.g., <u>montelukast</u>)

* Biologic agents (e.g., <u>dupilumab</u>)

* Polyp removal

* In patients with <u>AERD</u>: <u>aspirin</u> desensitization, followed by treatment with <u>aspirin</u>





> [!TIP]
> Polyp recurrence is common after <u>surgery</u>; continue pharmacological management after polyp removal. [[8]](/library/ytddT70)

### Fungal rhinosinusitis [[4]](/library/mxbVCD)[[14]](/library/2oXTY_)[[15]](/library/D6X1M_)




* Definition: rhinosinusitis caused by a fungal <u>pathogen</u>  [[14]](/library/2oXTY_)

* Classified by:

* Duration: acute (< 4 weeks) and chronic (≥ 12 weeks)

* <u>Histopathology</u>: invasive (e.g., acute invasive fungal rhinosinusitis) or noninvasive (e.g., fungal ball, <u>allergic fungal rhinosinusitis</u>)

* <u>Risk factors</u>

* Sinus <u>surgery</u> or trauma may lead to fungal <u>colonization</u>.

* <u>Immunosuppression</u> (e.g., <u>immunodeficiency</u>, chronic <u>steroid</u> use) and uncontrolled <u>diabetes mellitus</u> are <u>risk factors</u> for invasive <u>fungal rhinosinusitis</u>.

* Clinical features 

* General symptoms: See “<u>Acute rhinosinusitis</u>.”

* Noninvasive <u>fungal rhinosinusitis</u> [[4]](/library/mxbVCD)

* Allergic fungal: features of <u>asthma</u> and other <u>atopic</u> manifestations

* Fungal <u>mycetoma</u>: unilateral complaints; usually involves the <u>maxillary sinus</u>

* <u>Acute invasive fungal rhinosinusitis</u> : <u>epistaxis</u> and dark <u>ulcers</u> on the septum, <u>palate</u> and turbinates; may be acutely ill with <u>altered mental status</u> [[4]](/library/mxbVCD)

* Diagnostics

* CT: Possible findings include fungal balls, bony <u>erosions</u>, and extra sinonasal spread. [[16]](/library/PKXWg_)[[17]](/library/-qXDaz)

* <u>MRI</u>: may be indicated to assess for <u>cranial</u> or orbital spread, especially in <u>acute invasive fungal rhinosinusitis</u>

* <u>Nasal endoscopy</u>: Findings indicating <u>acute invasive fungal rhinosinusitis</u> include pale <u>mucosa</u>, dark <u>necrotic</u> areas, and crusting/<u>ulcers</u>.

* Fungal culture

* <u>Biopsy</u>

* Management

* An ENT specialist should manage all cases of suspected <u>fungal rhinosinusitis</u>.

* Patients with <u>acute invasive fungal rhinosinusitis</u>

* Admit as an inpatient and consult ENT and ID services immediately.

* Treatment may include <u>surgical debridement</u> of <u>necrotic</u> tissue, systemic <u>antifungal</u> therapy (e.g., <u>amphotericin B</u>), and reversal of <u>immunosuppression</u> if possible. [[15]](/library/D6X1M_)





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Acute invasive fungal rhinosinusitis</u> is a life-threatening diagnosis with a <u>mortality rate</u> of 50–80%. If suspected, immediately admit the patient and consult ENT. [[15]](/library/D6X1M_)

---

## Diagnosis

### General principles [[1]](/library/ys0dxh)[[6]](/library/UG0bAh)[[16]](/library/PKXWg_)




* Acute viral/<u>bacterial rhinosinusitis</u> is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u>.

* Assess patients using <u>diagnostic criteria for acute rhinosinusitis</u>.

* Imaging is only required for patients with any of the following:

* <u>Red flags for rhinosinusitis</u>

* <u>Risk factors</u> for complications (e.g., <u>immunosuppression</u>, <u>diabetes</u>, history of facial trauma)

* <u>Recurrent ARS</u>

* <u>Diagnosis of chronic rhinosinusitis</u> is made based on <u>diagnostic criteria for chronic rhinosinusitis</u>, which include findings of inflammation on either: [[13]](/library/Y6Xnj_)[[18]](/library/yL1dZ30)

* <u>CT scan</u>

* Direct visualization

* Additional studies should be performed in the following cases:

* <u>CRS</u> or <u>recurrent ARS</u> (to rule out comorbid conditions that affect management)

* Treatment failure

* Diagnostic uncertainty





> [!TIP]
> A <u>clinical diagnosis</u> of <u>chronic sinusitis</u> should be confirmed with objective documentation of sinonasal inflammation, which can be accomplished via <u>anterior rhinoscopy</u>, <u>nasal endoscopy</u>, or <u>CT scan</u>. [[6]](/library/UG0bAh)




### Red flags for rhinosinusitis [[1]](/library/ys0dxh)[[6]](/library/UG0bAh)[[16]](/library/PKXWg_)




Patients with <u>red flag symptoms</u> require urgent imaging; ENT may recommend further diagnostic studies.




* <u>Focal neurologic deficits</u> (including <u>cranial nerve palsies</u>)

* Severe <u>headache</u>

* Facial <u>edema</u>

* <u>Altered mental status</u>

* Ophthalmic complications (e.g., blurred <u>vision</u>, <u>proptosis</u>, impaired <u>ocular movements</u>)

* <u>Fever</u> > 39Â°C (> 102.2Â°F) and/or that lasts > 3 days

* Symptoms not improving despite adequate <u>antibiotic therapy</u>





### Imaging [[6]](/library/UG0bAh)[[16]](/library/PKXWg_)[[18]](/library/yL1dZ30)




* CT maxillofacial with or without IV contrast 

* Indications [[18]](/library/yL1dZ30)

* <u>CRS</u> or <u>recurrent ARS</u>

* <u>Acute rhinosinusitis</u> in patients with <u>risk factors</u> for complications or <u>red flags for rhinosinusitis</u>

* Findings may include signs of:

* Rhinosinusitis: opacification, <u>mucosal</u> thickening, air-fluid levels, <u>soft tissue</u> swelling  [[17]](/library/-qXDaz)

* Complications: spread beyond the sinuses

* Underlying causes of <u>CRS</u>: e.g., anatomic abnormalities, osteomeatal obstruction, polyposis

* Aggressive fungal infection or <u>neoplasm</u>: e.g., osseous destruction, extrasinus extension, local invasion  [[6]](/library/UG0bAh)[[15]](/library/D6X1M_)

* <u>MRI</u> with and without IV contrast:   can be used to evaluate for intracranial or intraorbital involvement or to differentiate polyps from tumors [[6]](/library/UG0bAh)[[16]](/library/PKXWg_)[[18]](/library/yL1dZ30)

* <u>X-ray</u> sinuses

* No longer recommended due to limited <u>sensitivity</u> and <u>specificity</u>

* May show sinus opacification and <u>air-fluid levels</u>

### Direct visualization




Direct visualization is usually performed by ENT.




* Indications: evaluation of complicated rhinosinusitis, <u>recurrent ARS</u>, or <u>CRS</u>

* Modalities

* <u>Nasal endoscopy</u> (preferred)

* <u>Anterior rhinoscopy</u>

* Findings

* Signs of rhinosinusitis: <u>mucosal</u> <u>erythema</u>, <u>edema</u>, osteomeatal blockage with <u>purulent</u> drainage [[6]](/library/UG0bAh)

* Detection of structural abnormalities or masses, if present

* Signs of <u>fungal rhinosinusitis</u>: <u>necrosis</u>





> [!WARNING]
> Pale or dark <u>necrotic</u> <u>mucosa</u> with crusting or <u>ulcers</u> indicates <u>acute invasive fungal rhinosinusitis</u>, which is a <u>medical emergency</u>. [[19]](/library/VpXGo_)




> [!TIP]
> <u>Anterior rhinoscopy</u> may miss smaller polyps and/or more <u>posterior</u> disease because it only visualizes the <u>anterior</u> third of the nasal cavity. If <u>anterior rhinoscopy</u> findings are normal, perform <u>nasal endoscopy</u>. [[6]](/library/UG0bAh)




### Additional studies




* Evaluation for comorbid conditions: Perform for patients with <u>recurrent ARS</u> and <u>CRS</u>. [[6]](/library/UG0bAh)

* <u>Allergic rhinitis</u>: Consider <u>allergen testing</u>.  [[6]](/library/UG0bAh)

* <u>Clinical features of asthma</u>: Perform diagnostic studies for <u>asthma</u>.

* <u>Clinical features of cystic fibrosis</u>: Perform <u>diagnostic evaluation for cystic fibrosis</u>.  [[6]](/library/UG0bAh)

* <u>Otitis media</u>, <u>bronchiectasis</u>, or <u>pneumonia</u>

* Refer to immunologist for <u>immunodeficiency</u> evaluation. [[6]](/library/UG0bAh)

* If <u>primary ciliary dyskinesia</u> is suspected, refer to pulmonologist for <u>biopsy</u> and/or <u>genetic testing</u>. [[6]](/library/UG0bAh)

* Rheumatologic disorders: Choice of further studies depends on clinical features (e.g, <u>diagnostic evaluation for sarcoidosis</u>, workup for <u>vasculitic syndrome</u>).  [[13]](/library/Y6Xnj_)

* Bacterial/fungal cultures: Request in cases of treatment failure.

* <u>Biopsy</u> (endoscopic or surgical): to identify an underlying condition (including malignancies) and to enable classification  [[20]](/library/epXxo_)

---

## Treatment

### Approach to <u>treatment of rhinosinusitis</u> [[6]](/library/UG0bAh)




* <u>Acute rhinosinusitis</u>

* Uncomplicated <u>viral rhinosinusitis</u> is usually <u>self-limiting</u>.

* Uncomplicated <u>ABRS</u>

* Treat with <u>antibiotics</u> or, if follow-up is assured, observe for up to 7 days;   before initiating <u>antibiotics</u>.

* If symptoms worsen at any time or fail to improve with treatment, reconsider the diagnosis and initiate or switch <u>antibiotic</u> treatment.

* Complications of <u>ABRS</u>: Start IV <u>antibiotics</u> and consult ENT.

* <u>Acute invasive fungal rhinosinusitis</u>: Immediately consult ENT and consider ID consult for <u>antifungal</u> therapy (e.g., <u>amphotericin B</u>) and <u>surgery</u>.

* Episode of <u>recurrent ARS</u>: Treat as <u>ABRS</u> initially and involve ENT for further management. [[13]](/library/Y6Xnj_)[[21]](/library/a6XQj_)

* <u>Chronic rhinosinusitis</u>

* Treat acute exacerbations as <u>ABRS</u>.    [[13]](/library/Y6Xnj_)

* Advise nasal saline <u>irrigation</u> for symptomatic relief.

* Treat the underlying inflammation with <u>corticosteroids</u>.   [[13]](/library/Y6Xnj_)[[21]](/library/a6XQj_)

* All patients: intranasal for at least 8–12 weeks  [[6]](/library/UG0bAh)

* Patients with <u>nasal polyps</u> and severe symptoms: Consider addition of a short course (3 weeks) of oral therapy.  [[13]](/library/Y6Xnj_)

* If there is no response to medical management, or if <u>red flags for sinusitis</u> are present, refer to ENT.





> [!TIP]
> In patients with <u>CRS</u>, do not prescribe <u>antifungals</u> (topical or systemic) and only use systemic <u>antibiotics</u> for the treatment of acute exacerbations. [[6]](/library/UG0bAh)[[13]](/library/Y6Xnj_)[[21]](/library/a6XQj_)




### Symptomatic treatment [[1]](/library/ys0dxh)[[6]](/library/UG0bAh)




The following options may be offered to all patients with rhinosinusitis.




* Nasal saline <u>irrigation</u>

* <u>Oral analgesics</u>, e.g., <u>ibuprofen</u> DOSAGE or <u>acetaminophen</u> DOSAGE

* Intranasal <u>steroids</u>, e.g., <u>mometasone</u> DOSAGE  [[22]](/library/9MXNIA) [[6]](/library/UG0bAh)

* Decongestants, e.g., <u>oxymetazoline</u> DOSAGE





### <u>Antibiotic</u> treatment [[6]](/library/UG0bAh)




* Indications

* <u>Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis</u> (initially or if symptoms worsen or do not improve during observation)

* Episode of <u>recurrent bacterial rhinosinusitis</u>

* Acute exacerbation of <u>chronic rhinosinusitis</u>

* Regimens

* First-line <u>antibiotic therapy</u>: <u>amoxicillin</u>, with or without <u>clavulanate</u>

* Usual oral treatment duration for adults: 5–10 days  [[1]](/library/ys0dxh)[[6]](/library/UG0bAh)

* Consider <u>risk factors</u> for treatment failure when choosing an appropriate <u>antibiotic</u>.

* Increased risk of bacterial resistance

* Severity of infection

* Patient factors, including smoke exposure, age > 65 years, and comorbidities, e.g., <u>diabetes</u> or cardiac/hepatic/renal disease

* In case of treatment failure, switch to one of the recommended <u>antibiotic</u> regimens from a different class with broader coverage.

| <u>Penicillin</u> <u>allergy</u> | <br><br>* Non-<u>type I hypersensitivity</u> to <u>penicillin</u>  [[6]](/library/UG0bAh)<br><br>* <u>Clindamycin</u> DOSAGE [[23]](/library/yMXdrA)<br><br>* PLUS a third-generation <u>cephalosporin</u><br><br>* <u>Cefixime</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* OR <u>Cefpodoxime</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Type I hypersensitivity</u> to <u>penicillin</u><br><br>* <u>Doxycycline</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* OR a <u>respiratory fluoroquinolone</u> <br><br>* <u>Levofloxacin</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* OR <u>moxifloxacin</u> DOSAGE<br><br><br> | <br>* Any type of hypersensitivity to <u>penicillin</u><br><br>* Second- or third-generation <u>cephalosporins</u> <br><br>* Cefdinir DOSAGE<br><br>* OR <u>Cefpodoxime</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* OR <u>clindamycin</u> DOSAGE  PLUS <u>cefixime</u> DOSAGE [[1]](/library/ys0dxh)<br><br>* OR <u>levofloxacin</u> DOSAGE<br><br> |

### <u>Surgery</u> [[1]](/library/ys0dxh)[[13]](/library/Y6Xnj_)[[24]](/library/rqXf-_)




* Indications

* Evidence of structural abnormalities: e.g., polyps, masses, or anatomical obstructions

* Treatment failure or <u>complications of rhinosinusitis</u>

* <u>Acute invasive fungal rhinosinusitis</u>

* Objective

* Improving aeration through sinus opening and drainage

* <u>Debridement</u> of <u>necrotic</u> tissue or <u>abscess</u> drainage

* Correction/removal of anatomic obstructions

* Obtaining intraoperative cultures and <u>biopsy</u> for <u>histopathology</u> if the diagnosis remains unclear

---

## Complications

* Local spread

* Mucoceles

* <u>Osteomyelitis</u>, especially of the <u>frontal bone</u> (also known as Pott's puffy tumor): subperiosteal <u>abscess</u> with local <u>pain</u> and <u>edema</u> that requires <u>antibiotic</u> treatment and <u>surgery</u>

* Spread to the <u>orbit</u>

* Preseptal/<u>orbital cellulitis</u>

* <u>Orbital abscess</u>

* <u>Cavernous sinus thrombosis</u>

* <u>Cavernous sinus syndrome</u>

* Intracranial spread

* Subdural <u>abscess</u>: most common

* <u>Meningitis</u>

* <u>Brain abscess</u>

* Systemic complications

* <u>Bacteremia</u>/<u>sepsis</u>

* <u>Pneumonia</u>

* <u>Multiple organ failure</u>

* Untreated <u>chronic sinusitis</u> can lead to life-threatening complications, as may be seen in patients with <u>cystic fibrosis</u>.





> [!TIP]
> Orbital and intracranial <u>necrotic</u> spread is especially common in invasive <u>fungal sinusitis</u>.




References:[[25]](/library/oxb0xD)[[26]](/library/KxbUxD)




We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.
